question: How do random forests and boosting build state-of-the-art predictors as sums of regression trees, and how do they relate to GLMs, GAMs and the lasso?
contributions: Random forests: variance reduction by averaging deep, decorrelated trees (bootstrap + split-variable randomization), with OOB error, jackknife SEs, variable importance
Boosting: gradient boosting with squared-error and general loss, shrinkage, depth and interaction order, AdaBoost as exponential-loss stagewise fitting
Connections of boosting to GAMs and the lasso (lasso post-processing of trees)

results.claim: AdaBoost is forward-stagewise fitting with exponential loss; its output G is half the logit; binomial loss has linear left tail vs exponential's severe tail.

limits: Examples are the spam data and the ALS data only; no repeated runs or error bars; figure values are not printed as numbers.
Authors concede boosting needs careful CV tuning (B, d, shrinkage) whereas random forests are nearly automatic.
Uncorrected jackknife SE of a random forest is upward biased for finite B (p.330).
Chapter predates XGBoost/LightGBM-style implementations; it uses R randomForest and gbm only.
practices: Use B large enough for the forest to stabilise; it cannot overfit by adding trees (p.328).
Use m near sqrt(p) for classification and p/3 for regression, tuning little (p.327-328).
Use OOB error as a free cross-validation estimate (p.329-330).
Use a much larger B when estimating jackknife variances, or the bias-corrected estimate (p.330).
Choose boosting depth d by CV; d sets interaction order d-1 (p.335-337).
Use small shrinkage and more trees; it makes the fit less sensitive to the stopping point B (p.338).
Treat a random forest as a benchmark for a parametric model: a big gap means interactions are missing (p.347-348).
Use the lasso to post-select and reweight boosted trees (p.346-347).

terms.definition: Grow many deep regression trees to randomized versions of the training data, and average them.
Repeatedly grow shallow trees to the residuals, and hence build up an additive model consisting of a sum of trees.
Error of each observation predicted by averaging only trees whose bootstrap sample excluded it.
The quantity y f(x) for a -1/1 response; positive means correct classification.
Boosting with depth d=k gives a (k-1)th-order interaction model; a (k-1)th-order interaction is a k-way interaction.
L_E(y,f(x)) = exp[-y f(x)], minimised in the population by half the logit.

code.snippet: Random forest: for b in 1..B: bootstrap sample d*_b; grow maximal-depth tree sampling m of p features before each split; save tree and bootstrap frequencies. Fit = (1/B) sum_b tree_b(x0). OOB_i uses only trees with w*_bi = 0.
Gradient boosting, squared error: G0=0, r=y. For b=1..B: fit depth-d tree g~_b to (X,r) best-first; G_b = G_{b-1} + eps*g~_b; r_i = r_i - eps*g~_b(x_i).
Gradient boosting: r_i = -dL(y_i,eta_i)/d eta_i at eta_i=G_{b-1}(x_i); fit depth-d tree to r by least squares; G_b = G_{b-1} + eps*g(x;theta_b).
AdaBoost: w_i=1/n; err_b = sum w_i I[y_i != c_b(x_i)] / sum w_i; alpha_b = log[(1-err_b)/err_b]; w_i <- w_i exp(alpha_b I[y_i != c_b(x_i)]); G_b = sum alpha c; C_b = sign(G_b).
